title: Sustainable yield and overdraft for a groundwater subbasin
analysis:
MEMORANDUM: Sustainable Yield Estimate, Las Garzas Subbasin
Prepared for: Willow Bend Groundwater Sustainability Agency

This memorandum presents the long-term average water budget for the Las Garzas Subbasin and derives the sustainable yield that will anchor the GSA's pumping reduction program. All values are average annual volumes for the 2001 to 2020 base period, which spans two wet cycles and two multi-year droughts and is representative of long-term hydrology.

Inflows to the groundwater system:
Deep percolation of precipitation: 14,500 acre-feet per year (AFY)
Streambed seepage from Las Garzas Creek (calibrated integrated model): 31,000 AFY
Return flow from applied irrigation water: 22,000 AFY
Subsurface inflow from the Sierra Fria foothills boundary: 19,500 AFY
Managed recharge at the Coyote Flats spreading grounds: 6,500 AFY
Channel losses measured between the Upper and Lower Las Garzas Creek gages: 21,000 AFY

Total inflow is 114,500 AFY.

Outflows other than pumping:
Subsurface outflow to the adjacent Arroyo Seco Subbasin: 11,000 AFY
Evapotranspiration by phreatophytes along the creek corridor: 6,000 AFY

Non-pumping outflow totals 17,000 AFY.

Sustainable yield is defined here as the average annual pumping that can be sustained with no long-term change in groundwater storage. Setting the change in storage to zero, sustainable yield equals total inflow minus non-pumping outflow: 114,500 AFY minus 17,000 AFY, or 97,500 AFY.

Average groundwater pumping over the base period was 112,000 AFY, based on metered municipal production and satellite-derived agricultural consumptive use converted to applied water. The resulting average overdraft is 112,000 AFY minus 97,500 AFY, or 14,500 AFY, which is 12.9 percent of current pumping.

Two cross-checks support these values. First, the base period begins and ends in similar hydrologic conditions (water years 2001 and 2020 were both near-median), so the average does not carry a wet-start or dry-end bias. Second, return flow of 22,000 AFY is 19.6 percent of pumping, which is within the typical range for a basin with mixed furrow, sprinkler, and drip irrigation.

Recommendation: An overdraft of 14,500 AFY can be corrected with a uniform reduction of roughly 13 percent in pumping phased over the 2025 to 2040 implementation period. This is a moderate adjustment that the GSA can achieve through its existing allocation framework, supplemented by modest expansion of the Coyote Flats recharge program. Larger reductions or demand-management measures such as land fallowing are not required to achieve sustainability by 2040.

error.location_quote: Channel losses measured between the Upper and Lower Las Garzas Creek gages: 21,000 AFY
error.explanation: Gaged channel loss on Las Garzas Creek is a measurement of the same physical process as the model-estimated streambed seepage from Las Garzas Creek; listing both as separate inflows counts creek recharge twice.
error.correct_reasoning: Keep one estimate of creek seepage (31,000 AFY). Total inflow = 14,500 + 31,000 + 22,000 + 19,500 + 6,500 = 93,500 AFY; sustainable yield = 93,500 - 17,000 = 76,500 AFY; overdraft = 112,000 - 76,500 = 35,500 AFY, or 31.7 percent of pumping, holding return flow fixed as the memo does. (If the gaged 21,000 AFY is kept instead and the modeled 31,000 AFY dropped, sustainable yield is 66,500 AFY and overdraft 45,500 AFY; either way overdraft is at least 35,500 AFY.)
error.impact: Overdraft is about 2.4 times larger (35,500 vs 14,500 AFY); a ~32 percent pumping reduction is needed, so the conclusion that a modest 13 percent cut suffices and fallowing is unnecessary is wrong.

grading_notes: Correct if the judge identifies that the gaged channel losses and the streambed seepage from the same creek are the same inflow counted twice (or equivalent: creek recharge double counted), inflating sustainable yield. Generic doubts about the base period, return-flow fraction, or model uncertainty do not count.

title: Minimum threshold exceedance and undesirable result determination
analysis:
MEMORANDUM: Chronic Lowering of Groundwater Levels, Fall 2025 Assessment
Prepared for: Board of Directors, Sierra Fria Groundwater Authority (Arroyo Blanco Subbasin)

Purpose. This memorandum evaluates fall 2025 groundwater level measurements against the sustainable management criteria for chronic lowering of groundwater levels adopted in the Arroyo Blanco Groundwater Sustainability Plan.

Adopted criteria. The Plan establishes a minimum threshold (MT) and measurable objective (MO) at each of 24 representative monitoring wells. Per Section 3.4 of the Plan, an undesirable result for chronic lowering occurs when groundwater levels fall below their minimum thresholds in at least 25 percent of representative monitoring wells (6 or more of 24) for two consecutive fall measurements.

Fall 2025 results. Fall 2025 measurements were collected between October 6 and October 24, 2025, after irrigation pumping had largely ceased, consistent with the Plan's monitoring protocol. Of the 24 representative wells:
7 wells (29.2 percent) were below their MT;
8 wells (33.3 percent) were between their MT and MO;
9 wells (37.5 percent) were at or above their MO.

The largest exceedance was at RMS-14 in the southern management area, where the measured groundwater elevation of 196.8 ft above mean sea level (msl) was 4.2 ft below the MT of 201.0 ft msl and 10.6 ft below the MO of 207.4 ft msl. Five of the seven exceedances are in the southern management area, where agricultural pumping is concentrated.

Comparison to fall 2024. In fall 2024, 3 of 24 representative wells (12.5 percent) were below their MT, so the number of wells in exceedance has more than doubled in one year.

Finding. With 29.2 percent of representative monitoring wells below their minimum thresholds in fall 2025, the 25 percent trigger in Section 3.4 has been exceeded. The Arroyo Blanco Subbasin is therefore experiencing an undesirable result for chronic lowering of groundwater levels as of fall 2025.

Recommended actions. Because an undesirable result has occurred, staff recommends that the Board (1) report the undesirable result in the April 2026 Annual Report, (2) immediately implement the Tier 2 pumping reductions of 15 percent in the southern management area specified in the Plan for undesirable-result conditions, and (3) direct staff to evaluate whether the MTs at RMS-14 and neighboring wells protect shallow domestic wells, since several domestic wells in the southern area have screens within 20 ft of the current water table. The 2026 monitoring schedule should also be expanded to include spring measurements at all 24 wells.

error.location_quote: The Arroyo Blanco Subbasin is therefore experiencing an undesirable result for chronic lowering of groundwater levels as of fall 2025.
error.explanation: The adopted definition requires MT exceedance at 25 percent or more of wells for two consecutive fall measurements. Fall 2024 had only 12.5 percent (3 of 24), so only one qualifying fall has occurred.
error.correct_reasoning: Fall 2024: 3/24 = 12.5 percent (below trigger); fall 2025: 7/24 = 29.2 percent (above trigger). One of two required consecutive measurements is met; an undesirable result would occur only if fall 2026 also shows 6 or more of 24 wells below MT.
error.impact: No undesirable result has yet occurred; the Tier 2 reductions keyed to undesirable-result conditions are not triggered by the Plan's own definition (the GSA may still act voluntarily), and the Annual Report should describe an exceedance trend, not an undesirable result.

grading_notes: Correct if the judge notes the two-consecutive-fall requirement is not met because fall 2024 was 12.5 percent. Objections about the MT values, domestic well protection, or the monitoring window are not the planted error.

title: Cooper-Jacob well interference at a neighboring domestic well
analysis:
MEMORANDUM: Well Interference Evaluation, Proposed Irrigation Well PW-3
Prepared for: Permitting Committee, Cañada Verde Groundwater Sustainability Agency

Request. Rancho Tierra Alta has applied to construct irrigation well PW-3, screened in the confined Valle Hondo aquifer, with a design pumping rate of 1,500 gallons per minute (gpm) during a 30-day peak irrigation period. The nearest existing well is the Ortega domestic well, 800 ft from PW-3 and screened in the same aquifer. Under the GSA's well permitting ordinance, a new well may not reduce the pump submergence of an existing well below 10 ft during a 30-day continuous pumping period.

Aquifer parameters. A 72-hour constant-rate test at the adjacent municipal well MW-2 in 2023, analyzed with the Cooper-Jacob straight-line method and checked against the Theis type curve, gives a transmissivity (T) of 12,000 square feet per day (ft^2/d) and a storativity (S) of 4 x 10^-4, consistent with confined conditions.

Pumping rate conversion. 1,500 gpm x 1,440 minutes per day / 7.4805 gallons per cubic foot = 288,750 cubic feet per day (ft^3/d).

Validity of the Cooper-Jacob approximation. The dimensionless time parameter is u = r^2 S / (4 T t) = (800 ft)^2 (4 x 10^-4) / (4 x 12,000 ft^2/d x 30 d) = 1.78 x 10^-4. Because u is well below 0.01, the Cooper-Jacob approximation matches the Theis solution closely (within about 0.1 percent here).

Predicted interference drawdown at the Ortega well after 30 days:
s = (2.3 Q / 4 pi T) log10(2.25 T t / (r^2 S))
2.3 Q / (4 pi T) = 2.3 x 288,750 / (4 pi x 12,000) = 4.40 ft
2.25 T t / (r^2 S) = 2.25 x 12,000 x 30 / (640,000 x 4 x 10^-4) = 3,164; log10(3,164) = 3.50
s = 4.40 ft x 3.50 = 15.4 ft

Effect on the Ortega well. The Ortega well's late-summer static water level is 142 ft below ground surface (bgs), its pump intake is set at 175 ft bgs, and its own pumping drawdown at 12 gpm is 1.5 ft, giving 31.5 ft of operating submergence. Subtracting the 15.4 ft of interference leaves 16.1 ft of submergence, above the 10 ft ordinance limit.

The analysis is conservative: it assumes 30 days of continuous pumping with no recovery and neglects aquitard leakage, which would reduce drawdown.

Conclusion. At 1,500 gpm, PW-3 is predicted to lower water levels at the Ortega well by about 15 ft over a 30-day peak period, leaving roughly 16 ft of pump submergence, which satisfies the ordinance. Staff recommends approval, with a transducer at the Ortega well during the first season.
grading_notes: Correct verdict: no material error. The gpm-to-ft^3/d conversion, u check, Cooper-Jacob drawdown (about 15.4 ft), and submergence arithmetic (175 - 142 - 1.5 = 31.5; 31.5 - 15.4 = 16.1 ft) are all right. Likely false alarms: using the Cooper-Jacob approximation at 800 ft (valid because u = 1.78e-4 < 0.01) and the small confined storativity of 4e-4 (appropriate for a confined aquifer; flagging it as too small is not an error).

title: Managed aquifer recharge credit accounting
analysis:
MEMORANDUM: Recharge Credit for the 2026 Diversion, Los Alisos Recharge Basin
Prepared for: Finance Committee, Valle del Sol Groundwater Sustainability Agency

Background. The GSA completed the Los Alisos Recharge Basin in 2025 at a capital cost of $1.9 million. The 14-acre basin receives high flows diverted from Alisos Creek under a temporary permit. Under the GSA's Recharge Credit Policy, recharge that reaches the aquifer is credited to the participating landowners' groundwater accounts, less a 10 percent leave-behind dedicated to the basin, and credits are valued at the GSA's adopted replacement water price of $350 per acre-foot (AF).

2026 diversion. Diversions occurred between January 12 and March 4, 2026 (52 days). The magnetic flowmeter at the diversion structure recorded a cumulative volume of 390 million gallons for the season, equivalent to 8,953 AF. The meter was calibrated in December 2025 and the readings were checked against the daily staff gauge record at the basin inlet.

Losses. The basin held standing water on 41 of the 52 days. Evaporation from the ponded surface, computed from the nearby CIMIS reference station and a pan coefficient appropriate for open water, totaled 4 AF. No surface outflow left the basin, as the outlet weir was closed for the entire season, and monitoring well LA-2 adjacent to the basin showed a water-level rise of 11 ft, consistent with the remaining water infiltrating to the aquifer.

Recharge accounting.
Gross diversion: 8,953 AF
Less evaporation: 4 AF
Net recharge: 8,949 AF
Less 10 percent leave-behind: 895 AF
Creditable recharge: 8,054 AF

Value of credits. At $350 per AF, the 8,054 AF of creditable recharge is worth $2.82 million. The 895 AF leave-behind adds a further 895 AF to basin storage, offsetting about 6 percent of the subbasin's estimated 15,000 AFY overdraft in a single season.

Findings.
1. The 2026 diversion season was the first full season of operation, and the basin performed as designed with no maintenance shutdowns.
2. The value of credits generated in a single season ($2.82 million in avoided replacement water purchases by participants) exceeds the full $1.9 million capital cost of the project, so the basin's first-year benefit to participants exceeded its full cost.
3. Because recharge was measured at the diversion meter and losses were directly estimated, the credited volume meets the Policy's measurement standard without the need for a separate infiltration study.

Recommendation. Staff recommends that the Committee (1) approve posting of 8,054 AF of recharge credits to participant accounts, and (2) authorize design of a second basin of similar size on the adjacent parcel, given the demonstrated first-year benefit.

error.location_quote: The magnetic flowmeter at the diversion structure recorded a cumulative volume of 390 million gallons for the season, equivalent to 8,953 AF.
error.explanation: 390 million gallons was converted to acre-feet using 43,560 (cubic feet per acre-foot) instead of 325,851 (gallons per acre-foot), overstating the volume by a factor of about 7.5.
error.correct_reasoning: 390,000,000 / 325,851 = 1,196.9 AF gross. Like the memo, this treats all infiltrated water as reaching the aquifer. Net of 4 AF evaporation = 1,192.9 AF; leave-behind 119.3 AF; creditable recharge 1,073.6 AF, worth about $376,000 at $350/AF. Leave-behind offsets under 1 percent (0.8 percent) of a 15,000 AFY overdraft.
error.impact: Credits are about $0.38 million, not $2.82 million; first-year benefit is about one-fifth of the capital cost rather than exceeding it, and posting 8,054 AF of credits would over-credit participants by about 6,980 AF.

grading_notes: Correct if the judge flags the gallons-to-acre-feet conversion (should divide by 325,851, giving about 1,197 AF) or equivalently shows the volume is about 7.5 times too high. Noting only that 8,953 AF on 14 acres implies an implausible infiltration rate, without tying it to the unit conversion, does not count; neither do complaints about the leave-behind policy or evaporation estimate.

title: Corbin Avenue storm drain capacity, City of Halvern Bay
analysis:
Drainage Capacity Assessment: Corbin Avenue Storm Drain, City of Halvern Bay

Purpose. Counsel for the owners of the commercial parcel at 410 Corbin Avenue asked whether the municipal storm drain fronting the property had sufficient capacity to convey the City's design storm and the rainfall that occurred on the night of the January 14 flooding event.

Drainage area. The tributary watershed to the Corbin Avenue inlet was delineated from the City's 2-ft contour mapping and verified in the field. It consists of mixed commercial and multifamily land use and measures 653,400 square feet in GIS. The tributary area of 653,400 square feet converts to 1.5 acres. A composite runoff coefficient of 0.80 was adopted, consistent with the City Drainage Manual table for dense commercial land use and confirmed by aerial imagery showing roughly 85 percent impervious cover.

Design storm. The City Drainage Manual requires local storm drains to convey the 10-year storm. Time of concentration was computed at 12 minutes (an inlet time of 8 minutes plus 4 minutes of gutter flow), and the corresponding 10-year intensity from the County intensity-duration-frequency curve is 4.2 inches per hour.

Peak flow. Applying the Rational Method, Q = C i A = 0.80 x 4.2 in/hr x 1.5 acres = 5.04 cfs.

Pipe capacity. The Corbin Avenue main is an 18-inch reinforced concrete pipe at a surveyed slope of 1.0 percent. Using Manning's equation with n = 0.013, a full-flow area of 1.767 square feet, and a hydraulic radius of 0.375 ft, full-flow capacity is Q = (1.49/0.013) x 1.767 x (0.375)^(2/3) x (0.010)^(1/2) = 10.53 cfs. The design peak is therefore about 48 percent of full-flow capacity, leaving a margin of approximately 5.5 cfs.

Rainfall on the event night. The nearest County gauge, Station HB-7, recorded a peak intensity of 3.4 inches per hour over the critical 12-minute duration, which is below the 10-year design intensity. The event peak flow would have been 0.80 x 3.4 x 1.5 = 4.08 cfs, or roughly 39 percent of pipe capacity.

Opinion. Based on these calculations, the Corbin Avenue storm drain had adequate hydraulic capacity both for the City's 10-year design standard and for the rainfall actually observed on January 14. Pipe capacity was not a cause of the flooding at 410 Corbin Avenue. The water that entered the building more likely originated from a localized source, such as a blocked inlet grate or an on-site drainage deficiency, and I recommend that further investigation focus there.

error.location_quote: The tributary area of 653,400 square feet converts to 1.5 acres.
error.explanation: 653,400 sq ft divided by 43,560 sq ft per acre is 15.0 acres, not 1.5 acres. The area is understated by a factor of 10, which propagates into both peak-flow estimates.
error.correct_reasoning: A = 653,400 / 43,560 = 15.0 acres. Design Q = 0.80 x 4.2 x 15.0 = 50.4 cfs; event Q = 0.80 x 3.4 x 15.0 = 40.8 cfs. Pipe capacity is 10.53 cfs, so design flow is about 4.8 times capacity and event flow about 3.9 times capacity.
error.impact: The conclusion reverses: the 18-inch main was severely undersized for both the 10-year design storm and the January 14 rainfall, so pipe capacity is a likely contributor to the flooding rather than being ruled out.

grading_notes: Correct identification must flag the square-feet-to-acres conversion (15 acres, not 1.5) and note that peak flow then far exceeds the 10.53 cfs pipe capacity. Generic criticism of the runoff coefficient, the omitted 1.008 factor, or the time of concentration does not count.

title: Sorrel Road culvert capacity under backwater, Dunmore County
analysis:
Culvert Hydraulic Review: Sorrel Road Crossing, Wexham Creek Tributary, Dunmore County

Assignment. I was retained to evaluate whether the County's culvert under Sorrel Road had capacity to pass runoff from the March 3 storm, or whether flooding of the Lindqvist residence immediately upstream resulted from other factors.

Watershed and peak flow. The tributary watershed is 44.4 acres of rural residential land. Using a runoff coefficient of 0.45 and the 25-year, 30-minute intensity of 2.9 in/hr from the County intensity-duration-frequency curve (time of concentration of 30 minutes by the Kirpich method), the Rational Method peak is Q = 0.45 x 2.9 x 44.4 = 57.9 cfs. Gauge records indicate the March 3 storm was approximately a 25-year event at that duration, so 57.9 cfs is adopted as the event peak inflow.

Culvert geometry. The crossing is a single 36-inch reinforced concrete pipe, 120 ft long, with an inlet invert of 101.2 ft and an outlet invert of 100.0 ft (NAVD88), giving a barrel slope of 0.010 ft/ft. The inlet is a square-edged headwall with an entrance loss coefficient of 0.5. Field inspection on March 5 found the barrel clean, with less than 1 inch of sediment and no structural defects.

Survey data. The lowest finished floor of the Lindqvist residence is at 105.5 ft, and interior water lines show flooding to that elevation and slightly above. At the culvert outlet, debris lines on the downstream channel banks place the peak stage at 103.9 ft, reflecting backwater from Wexham Creek, which was in flood that afternoon.

Capacity. For a circular pipe flowing full, the flow area is 7.069 square feet and the hydraulic radius is 0.75 ft. The barrel capacity was computed with Manning's equation for full flow at the barrel slope: Q = (1.49/0.013) x 7.069 x (0.75)^(2/3) x (0.010)^(1/2) = 66.9 cfs. This exceeds the event peak inflow by 9.0 cfs, a margin of about 16 percent.

Opinion. Because the capacity of the Sorrel Road culvert (66.9 cfs) exceeds the March 3 peak inflow (57.9 cfs), the culvert was hydraulically adequate for the event and did not cause water to pond upstream of Sorrel Road to the elevation of the Lindqvist finished floor. The flooding of the residence is more reasonably attributed to overland flow from the adjacent hillside and to the low floor elevation of the home relative to the tributary floodplain. The culvert is clean, structurally sound, and sized consistent with the 25-year criterion applied by the County to rural road crossings, and I find no hydraulic deficiency attributable to the County.

error.location_quote: The barrel capacity was computed with Manning's equation for full flow at the barrel slope: Q = (1.49/0.013) x 7.069 x (0.75)^(2/3) x (0.010)^(1/2) = 66.9 cfs.
error.explanation: The memo's own data show the outlet was submerged: tailwater at 103.9 ft is 0.9 ft above the outlet crown (100.0 + 3.0 = 103.0 ft). Under that tailwater the culvert operates in outlet control, and capacity depends on the headwater minus tailwater difference and the entrance, friction, and exit losses, not on Manning normal-depth flow at the barrel slope.
error.correct_reasoning: Outlet control, full flow: H = [1 + ke + 29 n^2 L / R^(4/3)] V^2/2g = [1 + 0.5 + 29(0.013^2)(120)/0.75^(4/3)] V^2/2g = 2.36 V^2/2g. With headwater limited to the finished floor (105.5 ft) and tailwater at 103.9 ft, H = 1.6 ft, V = 6.60 ft/s, Q = 46.7 cfs, below the 57.9 cfs inflow. Passing 57.9 cfs requires H = 2.46 ft, i.e., headwater of about 106.4 ft, roughly 0.9 ft above the finished floor.
error.impact: Under the observed tailwater the culvert could pass only about 47 cfs without raising headwater above the finished floor; passing the event peak required headwater near 106.4 ft. The culvert (under backwater) therefore explains ponding to the floor elevation, and the opinion that it was adequate and played no role is unsupported.

grading_notes: Credit requires recognizing that the high tailwater (above the outlet crown) puts the culvert in outlet control so Manning full-flow capacity at barrel slope is the wrong basis, and that the head-limited capacity falls below 57.9 cfs. Vague remarks that 'tailwater was ignored' without linking it to reduced capacity, or challenges to C, intensity, or n, are near-misses that do not count.

title: Water main break vs. storm runoff, Ashgrove Lane basement flooding
analysis:
Source Attribution of Basement Flooding: 22 Ashgrove Lane, Town of Pelling

Background. On the evening of October 9, the Pelling Municipal Water Utility's 8-inch distribution main on Ashgrove Lane failed at a joint approximately 60 ft upslope of 22 Ashgrove Lane. The homeowners' finished basement flooded the same evening. Counsel asked me to determine the source of the floodwater.

Main break discharge. Utility SCADA records show a pressure drop in the Ashgrove pressure zone at 21:40, and the repair crew closed the isolation valves at 23:15, a release duration of 95 minutes. Based on the pressure loss and the opening at the separated joint, the utility estimated a discharge of 1,150 gpm. Released volume = 1,150 gpm x 95 min = 109,250 gallons, or 14,605 cubic feet at 7.4805 gallons per cubic foot.

Flooded volume. The basement has a floor area of 1,950 square feet. Water lines on drywall, photographed on October 10 and measured during my site visit, show a maximum depth of 3.2 ft. The flooded volume is therefore 1,950 x 3.2 = 6,240 cubic feet.

Pathway. The street crown and gutter on Ashgrove Lane slope toward the property, and the driveway descends to a below-grade exterior stairwell serving the basement door. The stairwell drain was found partly obstructed with leaf litter. Water arriving at the driveway apron has a direct path to the basement door.

Rainfall and timeline. A weather station at Pelling Middle School, 0.4 mile away, recorded 1.6 inches of rain between 18:00 and 22:00, including 0.9 inch in the hour ending 21:00. The 0.85-acre paved parking lot of the church upslope drains onto Ashgrove Lane above the residence. The homeowner's phone photograph of the stairwell, with metadata time 21:12, shows water flowing down the exterior stairs and about 4 inches of water on the basement floor. The homeowner called the utility at 21:52 to report water bubbling from the street.

Analysis. The released main-break volume of 14,605 cubic feet is 2.3 times the flooded basement volume of 6,240 cubic feet, so even if a majority of the release continued down the gutter past the property, the remaining fraction was more than sufficient to produce the observed depth. The break location upslope of the residence and on the same gutter line places the property directly in the discharge path.

Opinion. Because the main break released more than twice the volume needed to fill the basement to the observed depth, and the break occurred directly upslope of the residence, the water main failure is the cause of the basement flooding at 22 Ashgrove Lane.

error.location_quote: Because the main break released more than twice the volume needed to fill the basement to the observed depth, and the break occurred directly upslope of the residence, the water main failure is the cause of the basement flooding at 22 Ashgrove Lane.
error.explanation: The memo documents that water was already entering the basement at 21:12, 28 minutes before the main failed at 21:40, during intense rainfall with an upslope paved lot draining along the same pathway, yet attributes the flooding solely to the main break. Volume sufficiency of the main release does not exclude storm runoff as a cause.
error.correct_reasoning: Storm runoff from the church lot alone is about 0.85 ac x 43,560 sq ft/ac x (1.6/12) ft x 0.90 = 4,443 cubic feet, equivalent to about 71 percent of the 6,240 cubic feet in the basement if most of it reaches the stairwell, before counting street and roof runoff. The volume argument also requires at least 42.7 percent of the main release (6,240 / 14,605 cubic feet) to have reached the basement, which the memo does not show. Flooding was underway (about 4 inches) before the break, so storm runoff is at least a substantial and possibly dominant contributor; the main break may have added to the depth after 21:40, but attribution requires apportionment between the two sources.
error.impact: The sole-cause attribution to the water main is not supported; the correct opinion is that storm runoff initiated the flooding and the main break was a contributing source whose share requires apportionment, which materially changes liability and damages allocation.

grading_notes: Credit requires pointing to the 21:12 photo (flooding before the 21:40 break) and/or the rainfall runoff pathway as an unaddressed competing cause that defeats the sole-cause opinion. Merely questioning the utility's 1,150 gpm estimate or the conversion factor does not count.

title: Fenwick Street storm drain adequacy and event frequency (control)
analysis:
Storm Drain Adequacy and Event Frequency: Fenwick Street, City of Arlow Mesa

Assignment. Counsel for the City asked me to evaluate whether the Fenwick Street storm drain met the City's 10-year design standard and to characterize the frequency of the November 18 storm, which plaintiffs' complaint describes as a "100-year storm."

Drainage area and runoff coefficient. The tributary area to the Fenwick Street inlet is 10.0 acres, delineated from City contour mapping. It comprises 6.2 acres of commercial frontage with a runoff coefficient of 0.90 and 3.8 acres of landscaped residential lots with a coefficient of 0.35. The area-weighted composite coefficient is C = (6.2 x 0.90 + 3.8 x 0.35) / 10.0 = (5.58 + 1.33) / 10.0 = 0.691.

Design peak flow. The time of concentration is 15 minutes, and the City intensity-duration-frequency curve gives a 10-year, 15-minute intensity of 3.1 in/hr. By the Rational Method, Q = 0.691 x 3.1 in/hr x 10.0 acres = 21.4 cfs. Consistent with standard practice, the unit conversion factor of 1.008 is taken as 1.

Pipe capacity. The Fenwick Street main is a 24-inch reinforced concrete pipe with a surveyed slope of 0.7 percent. With n = 0.013, a full-flow area of 3.142 square feet, and a hydraulic radius of 0.50 ft, Manning's equation gives Q = (1.49/0.013) x 3.142 x (0.50)^(2/3) x (0.007)^(1/2) = 19.0 cfs. The 10-year design peak exceeds full-flow capacity by about 2.4 cfs, or about 13 percent of full-flow capacity, and also exceeds the maximum partial-flow capacity of about 20.4 cfs.

Event frequency. The City gauge at Fenwick Yard recorded a maximum 15-minute intensity of 3.1 in/hr on November 18, matching the 10-year value, not the 100-year value. This duration equals the time of concentration and therefore governs peak flow in this drain. A 10-year storm has an annual exceedance probability of 10 percent. Over a 30-year service life, the probability of at least one such event is 1 - (1 - 0.10)^30 = 95.8 percent. For comparison, the probability of at least one 100-year event in 30 years is 1 - (0.99)^30 = 26.0 percent.

Opinion. The Fenwick Street main is modestly undersized relative to the City's 10-year standard, with full-flow capacity about 11 percent below the design peak; at the design peak the pipe could not carry the flow under gravity (open-channel) conditions. At the governing 15-minute duration, the November 18 storm was approximately a 10-year event, not a 100-year event, and an event of that magnitude was highly likely to occur during the service life of the system. Whether surcharging caused flooding at any particular property depends on a hydraulic grade line analysis of the full system, which is outside the scope of this memorandum.
grading_notes: Correct verdict is no material error: C = 0.691, Q = 21.4 cfs, full-flow capacity = 19.0 cfs (the design peak is about 13 percent above full-flow capacity, which is about 11 percent below the peak, and above the roughly 20.4 cfs maximum partial-flow capacity, so the pipe cannot convey it as gravity flow), and 95.8 percent and 26.0 percent exceedance probabilities all check. Features that look suspicious but are fine: taking the 1.008 factor as 1, judging frequency at the 15-minute duration only (explicitly justified as the duration equal to the time of concentration), and a 10-year storm having a 95.8 percent chance of occurring in 30 years.

title: Contract diversion accounting, Larkspur Creek
analysis:
Expert Report Excerpt: Reconstruction of 2025 Season Diversions, Tamsen Valley Water Company v. Halloway Ranch

Contract terms. Under the 2019 Water Supply Agreement, Halloway Ranch may divert up to 980 acre-feet (AF) from Larkspur Creek during the April 1 through September 30 irrigation season. Diversions above that amount are compensable at the contract rate of $410 per AF.

Diversion facilities and records. I reconstructed season diversions from the records produced by both parties and from my site inspection. Water is taken from Larkspur Creek at Station A, an electric pump station with a magnetic flowmeter. Station A discharges into a manifold that splits flow between the Upper Lateral and the Eastside Lateral. The Eastside Lateral carries a Parshall flume with a stage logger roughly 400 ft below the manifold. Separately, a portable diesel pump (Pump B) draws directly from the creek to irrigate the lower field and is not metered.

Station A. The flowmeter record shows an average rate of 2.45 cfs over the 183-day season. Volume = 2.45 cfs x 183 days x 1.983 AF per cfs-day = 889.1 AF. Gaps in the record total 31 hours and were filled by linear interpolation; the result is insensitive to this fill (under 0.5 AF).

Pump B. Fuel purchase records and the ranch foreman's daily sheets support 1,200 hours of operation. The manufacturer's pump curve gives an output of 280 gpm at the observed total dynamic head. Volume = 280 gpm x 60 min/hr x 1,200 hr / 325,851 gal/AF = 61.9 AF.

Eastside Lateral flume. The flume stage logger yields an average flow of 310 gpm during 1,450 hours of recorded flow. Volume = 310 gpm x 60 min/hr x 1,450 hr / 325,851 gal/AF = 82.8 AF. A spot check with a portable acoustic meter on August 12 agreed with the flume rating within 4 percent.

Season total. Total season diversion = 889.1 + 61.9 + 82.8 = 1,033.8 AF. This exceeds the 980 AF contract limit by 53.8 AF, or 5.5 percent. At the contract rate of $410 per AF, the volume diverted in excess of the limit corresponds to $22,058.

Opinion. Based on the metered and reconstructed records, Halloway Ranch diverted approximately 1,034 AF from Larkspur Creek during the 2025 irrigation season, exceeding its 980 AF contractual entitlement by approximately 54 AF. The Pump B estimate carries the largest uncertainty, but a plausible range of pump output (plus or minus 10 percent) changes the total by only about 6 AF and does not alter the conclusion that the limit was exceeded.

error.explanation: The Eastside Lateral flume measures water downstream of the Station A manifold, so its 82.8 AF is a subset of the 889.1 AF already metered at Station A. Adding it counts that water twice.
error.correct_reasoning: Creek diversions occur only at Station A and Pump B: 889.1 + 61.9 = 951.0 AF. The flume volume (82.8 AF, about 9.3 percent of Station A) is an internal distribution measurement, useful only as a cross-check. 951.0 AF is 29.0 AF below the 980 AF limit; even with Pump B at plus 10 percent (about 6 AF), the total stays below the limit.
error.impact: The conclusion reverses: corrected diversions of about 951 AF are within the 980 AF entitlement, so there is no overdiversion and the $22,058 figure has no basis.

grading_notes: Credit requires identifying that the flume on the Eastside Lateral measures water already counted at Station A (double counting) and that removing it brings the total below 980 AF. Challenging the unmetered Pump B estimate, the interpolation, or the cfs-day conversion is a near-miss that does not count.

title: TCE well contamination causation opinion, Garrow Flats
analysis:
Expert Report Excerpt: Source of TCE in Garrow Flats Mutual Water Company Well 3

Assignment. Counsel for Garrow Flats Mutual Water Company asked me to evaluate whether trichloroethylene (TCE) detected in the company's Well 3 originated from the documented November 10, 2015 solvent release at the former Pellham Fine Cleaners facility.

Site setting. The facility lies 1,050 ft hydraulically upgradient of Well 3 in an unconfined sand and gravel aquifer. Water-level contour maps from eight monitoring wells show a consistent horizontal gradient of 0.004 ft/ft directed from the facility toward Well 3 in all four quarterly events reviewed. Effective porosity of 0.25 was adopted from grain-size analyses of six soil cores.

Hydraulic conductivity. Six slug tests in the aquifer yielded hydraulic conductivity values ranging from 18 to 70 ft/day, with a median of 45 ft/day. I adopted the median as the representative value.

Travel time. Average linear groundwater velocity is v = K i / n = 45 x 0.004 / 0.25 = 0.72 ft/day. Advective travel time over 1,050 ft is 1,050 / 0.72 = 1,458 days, or 4.0 years. Measured fraction of organic carbon in the cores is low (0.0003). With a TCE organic carbon partition coefficient of 94 L/kg, a bulk density of 1.75 g/cm3, and a total porosity of 0.32, the retardation factor is R = 1 + (1.75 / 0.32) x 94 x 0.0003 = 1.154, which extends travel time to 1,458 x 1.154 = 1,683 days, or 4.6 years. Starting from the November 10, 2015 release, predicted advective arrival at Well 3 is June 2020.

Well 3 sampling record. Well 3 is sampled for volatile organic compounds on a three-year regulatory schedule. The August 2017 sample was non-detect for TCE at a reporting limit of 0.5 micrograms per liter. The August 2020 sample contained 14 micrograms per liter of TCE, above the 5 micrograms per liter maximum contaminant level, and confirmation sampling in September 2020 returned 16 micrograms per liter. Concentrations have since stabilized between 18 and 24 micrograms per liter.

Release documentation. The facility's 2015 incident report records a release of approximately 40 gallons of spent TCE-based solvent to an unpaved area behind the building, and the regional board's 2018 site investigation found TCE in facility soil gas at concentrations consistent with a substantial source.

Opinion. The predicted arrival of TCE at Well 3 in June 2020 matches the first detection in August 2020 to within two months, and the hydraulic gradient places the facility directly upgradient of the well. The agreement between predicted and observed arrival establishes, to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty, that the November 2015 release at Pellham Fine Cleaners is the sole source of TCE in Well 3 and excludes any other potential source.

error.location_quote: The agreement between predicted and observed arrival establishes, to a reasonable degree of scientific certainty, that the November 2015 release at Pellham Fine Cleaners is the sole source of TCE in Well 3 and excludes any other potential source.
error.explanation: The arithmetic is correct, but the timing 'match' is far weaker than claimed: the memo's own conductivity range gives arrival times of about 3 to 11.5 years, and triennial sampling only bounds first arrival somewhere between August 2017 and August 2020. Timing consistency and upgradient position can support 'consistent with' but cannot establish a sole source or exclude others, which were never investigated.
error.correct_reasoning: With retardation (R = 1.154) applied throughout: K = 70 ft/day gives v = 1.12 ft/day and travel time = 1,082 days (3.0 yr, arrival about October 2018); K = 18 ft/day gives v = 0.288 ft/day and travel time = 4,208 days (11.5 yr, arrival about 2027). These are advective travel times; dispersion can bring first arrival earlier. The observed record only shows arrival between August 2017 and August 2020. A defensible opinion is that the Pellham release is a plausible and likely contributing source whose timing is consistent with the data; sole-source attribution would require a source survey, plume delineation, or chemical fingerprinting.
error.impact: The opinion must be downgraded from exclusive, certain causation to 'consistent with and a probable contributor'; the 'excludes any other source' claim, which is the litigation-critical element, is unsupported.

grading_notes: Credit requires identifying that the sole-source, certainty, or 'excludes any other source' conclusion is overstated relative to the evidence, for example by citing the hydraulic conductivity range, the three-year sampling gap, or the lack of any evaluation of other sources. Disputing the retardation or velocity arithmetic (both are correct) does not count.

title: Pre and post development peak flow comparison, Cobble Creek
analysis:
MEMORANDUM: Change in Peak Flow on Cobble Creek Following the Larkspur Heights Development
Prepared for: Counsel for the Delmont Road Homeowners

Assignment. Counsel asked me to evaluate whether construction of the Larkspur Heights subdivision increased peak flows on Cobble Creek at the Delmont Road reach, where five residences flooded on January 14, 2023.

Watershed and development. Cobble Creek drains 2,960 acres upstream of Delmont Road. Larkspur Heights was graded and built between March 2020 and June 2022 on 640 acres in the upper watershed, or 21.6 percent of the drainage area. The approved site plan shows 62 percent impervious cover, so the project added about 396.8 acres of roofs and pavement. Its two detention basins were designed for the 10-year storm only.

Stream gauge record. The Halvern County Flood Control District installed stream gauge CC-2 on Cobble Creek at Ridgeway Road, 0.6 mile upstream of Delmont Road, in October 2021. CC-2 records stage every 15 minutes and converts stage to discharge with a rating curve checked by current-meter measurements in 2022 and 2023.

Rainfall. The Halvern Airport rain gauge, operated continuously since 1987 and 2.1 miles from the watershed centroid, recorded 3.52 inches in 24 hours during the January 14, 2023 storm. The February 2, 2019 storm produced 3.41 inches in 24 hours at the same gauge, so the 2023 storm delivered 3.2 percent more rainfall. Peak 1-hour rainfall was also similar: 0.88 inches in 2023 and 0.85 inches in 2019. Under the County's adopted depth-duration-frequency table, 3.52 inches in 24 hours is about a 25-year event. Both storms followed at least two weeks of wet antecedent conditions.

Paired storm comparison. CC-2 recorded a peak discharge of 640 cubic feet per second (cfs) on January 14, 2023. For the comparable predevelopment storm, CC-2 recorded a peak of 410 cfs on February 2, 2019. The postdevelopment peak is therefore 230 cfs higher, an increase of 56.1 percent, against a rainfall difference of only 3.2 percent. Rainfall depth alone cannot account for a change of this size.

Interpretation. The increase is consistent with the mechanisms expected from Larkspur Heights: faster runoff from 396.8 acres of new impervious surface, conveyance through storm drains rather than overland flow, and detention basins sized for the 10-year storm, smaller than the roughly 25-year January 2023 event. No other land-use change of comparable scale occurred in the watershed between 2019 and 2023, based on my review of county grading permits.

Opinion. Based on the paired storm comparison at CC-2, the Larkspur Heights development increased the peak flow of Cobble Creek at Delmont Road by approximately 56 percent for a storm of this size, and that increase was a substantial factor in the flooding of the Delmont Road residences on January 14, 2023.

error.location_quote: For the comparable predevelopment storm, CC-2 recorded a peak of 410 cfs on February 2, 2019.
error.explanation: The memo states that gauge CC-2 was installed in October 2021, so it cannot have recorded any discharge on February 2, 2019. The 410 cfs predevelopment peak does not exist as a measured value, and it is the sole basis for the 56 percent increase and the causation opinion.
error.correct_reasoning: CC-2 began recording in October 2021, after grading started in March 2020, so it has no predevelopment record at all. The comparison 640 - 410 = 230 cfs (56.1 percent) rests on a nonexistent observation. The only valid paired fact is rainfall (3.52 vs 3.41 inches, 3.2 percent more in 2023). A predevelopment peak would have to be estimated by other means, such as a calibrated rainfall-runoff model run with and without the 396.8 acres of added impervious cover, or a regional gauge with a pre-2020 record, and the opinion must wait for that analysis.
error.impact: The quantitative basis for the opinion disappears. The 56 percent increase and the substantial factor conclusion are unsupported until a legitimate predevelopment baseline is developed; presenting a nonexistent gauge reading in an expert opinion would also be impeachable on its face.

grading_notes: Correct only if the judge identifies that the 2019 CC-2 reading cannot exist because the gauge was installed in October 2021 (or equivalently, that there is no predevelopment record at CC-2), and that the conclusion depends on it. Near-misses that do not count: general doubts about comparing only two storms, antecedent moisture, rating curve accuracy, detention basin sizing, or the airport rain gauge's distance from the watershed. Arithmetic objections do not count; 230 cfs, 56.1 percent, 3.2 percent, 21.6 percent, and 396.8 acres are all correct. Generic objections that a single paired-storm comparison is limited, or that 24-hour depth does not capture intensity (the memo reports matched peak 1-hour rainfall), do not count.

title: Culvert adequacy opinion under a county design standard, Hollins Road
analysis:
Expert Report Excerpt: Hydraulic Adequacy of the Hollins Road Culvert
Prepared for: Counsel for the County of Marrowfield

Assignment. Counsel for the County retained me to evaluate the hydraulic capacity of the 54-inch corrugated metal pipe culvert that carries Tamsen Gulch under Hollins Road, in connection with flooding of three properties upstream of the road on December 3, 2024. Counsel anticipates that the analysis will show the culvert was adequately sized and that the flooding resulted from an extraordinary storm.

Design standard. Hollins Road is a collector road. Counsel asked me to apply the current Marrowfield County Drainage Design Manual. Its Section 5.2 requires culverts under collector roads to pass the 25-year peak flow without overtopping the roadway.

Design flow. The Tamsen Gulch watershed upstream of Hollins Road covers 110 acres of mixed residential and pasture land. Using the rational method with a runoff coefficient of 0.65 and the County's 25-year rainfall intensity of 2.6 inches per hour at the watershed time of concentration, Q = CiA = 0.65 x 2.6 x 110 = 185.9 cfs.

Culvert capacity. The roadway sag is 6.75 ft above the culvert invert, a headwater to diameter ratio of 1.5. From the inlet control nomograph for a 54-inch projecting corrugated metal pipe at that ratio, the culvert passes 142 cfs before the road overtops. Outlet control was checked and does not govern.

December 3, 2024 storm. The County's Hollins Yard rain gauge, 0.3 mile from the culvert, recorded a peak intensity of 2.1 inches per hour over the time of concentration, which corresponds to roughly the 10-year event in the County's intensity duration frequency curves. The resulting peak flow is 0.65 x 2.1 x 110 = 150.2 cfs, which is 105.8 percent of culvert capacity, an excess of 8.2 cfs. Witnesses and a County maintenance log confirm that Hollins Road overtopped for about 40 minutes. The culvert inlet was inspected the following morning and found free of debris.

Discussion. Rational method estimates carry recognized uncertainty in runoff coefficient and rainfall intensity, and the culvert was installed in 1988, before the current Manual edition. The December 2024 storm was an intense event that produced widespread nuisance flooding elsewhere in the County.

Opinion. Considering the intensity of the December 3, 2024 storm and the recognized uncertainty in rational method estimates, the Hollins Road culvert was adequately sized, and the flooding resulted from a storm that exceeded what the culvert could reasonably be expected to convey.

error.location_quote: Considering the intensity of the December 3, 2024 storm and the recognized uncertainty in rational method estimates, the Hollins Road culvert was adequately sized, and the flooding resulted from a storm that exceeded what the culvert could reasonably be expected to convey.
error.explanation: The memo's own correct calculations show the culvert fails the County's 25-year standard (142 cfs capacity vs 185.9 cfs required) and was overtopped by roughly a 10-year storm, which is smaller than the design storm. The conclusion adopts counsel's anticipated finding of adequacy and an extraordinary storm by leaning on generic uncertainty and the storm's intensity, neither of which closes the gap.
error.correct_reasoning: Capacity 142 cfs is 76.4 percent of the 25-year flow of 185.9 cfs, a 43.9 cfs shortfall, so the culvert does not meet Section 5.2. The December 2024 peak of 150.2 cfs (about a 10-year event, below the 25-year design event) exceeded capacity by 8.2 cfs, so a culvert meeting the standard would have passed it with about 35.7 cfs of margin (185.9 - 150.2). Rational method uncertainty applies equally in both directions and cannot convert a 23.6 percent capacity deficit into adequacy. The supportable opinion is that the culvert is undersized relative to the County standard and that the storm was within its design range. The memo states it applies the current Manual, so the 1988 installation date does not change this comparison.
error.impact: The opinion reverses: the memo's own numbers show the culvert was inadequate under the County's standard and was overtopped by a storm smaller than the design event, so the adequacy and extraordinary storm conclusions are unsupported.

grading_notes: Correct if the judge identifies that the conclusion of adequacy contradicts the memo's own numbers, citing the capacity shortfall (142 vs 185.9 cfs, or 76.4 percent) and/or that a roughly 10-year storm (below the 25-year design event) overtopped the road, and ideally notes the conclusion tracks counsel's stated expectation. Near-misses that do not count: disputing the runoff coefficient, the nomograph reading, or the rational method itself; raising the 1988 installation date alone; or flagging the client expectation in the assignment without showing the numbers contradict the conclusion. All arithmetic in the memo (185.9, 150.2, 105.8, 8.2, 1.5) is correct; 76.4 percent and 43.9 cfs appear only in the key.

title: PCE vapor intrusion from former dry cleaner, Oriel Court residences
analysis:
Expert Report Excerpt: Vapor Intrusion Evaluation, Former Pellmore Cleaners, 4410 Marlow Avenue

Assignment. Counsel for the owners of two single-family residences on Oriel Court asked me to evaluate whether tetrachloroethylene (PCE) vapors from the former Pellmore Cleaners present an unacceptable indoor air risk. Pellmore operated a dry cleaning machine in Unit 3 of the Marlow Avenue retail building from 1978 to 2009. The two residences, 418 and 422 Oriel Court, abut the rear property line, roughly 70 ft and 95 ft from the former machine location.

Sampling. In March I directed installation of sub-slab vapor probes beneath the slab of Unit 4 of the retail building (the space adjoining the former cleaner, now a print shop) and beneath the basement slabs of both residences. Samples were collected in 6-liter evacuated canisters over 30 minutes and analyzed by Method TO-15. Leak checks with helium were below 2 percent at all probes. Measured sub-slab PCE concentrations were 1,400 ug/m3 at Unit 4, 520 ug/m3 at 418 Oriel Court, and 610 ug/m3 at 422 Oriel Court. Using a PCE molecular weight of 165.83 g/mol, these correspond to 206.4, 76.7, and 89.9 ppbv, respectively (ppbv = ug/m3 x 24.45 / 165.83 at 25 C).

Attenuation. A sub-slab to indoor air attenuation factor of 0.03 was adopted for this evaluation. Predicted indoor air concentration equals the attenuation factor times the sub-slab concentration: 0.03 x 1,400 = 42.0 ug/m3 at Unit 4, 0.03 x 520 = 15.6 ug/m3 at 418 Oriel Court, and 0.03 x 610 = 18.3 ug/m3 at 422 Oriel Court.

Screening level. An indoor air screening level for PCE of 47 ug/m3 was adopted for this evaluation. That value corresponds to the target cancer risk and hazard quotient used throughout this report and assumes an occupant exposure of 8 hours per day, 250 days per year, for 25 years. The print shop operates on a single weekday shift.

Comparison. Predicted indoor air concentrations at all three structures are therefore below the 47 ug/m3 screening level adopted for this evaluation. The highest predicted value, 42.0 ug/m3 at Unit 4, is 89 percent of the screening level, and the residential predictions are 33 and 39 percent of it. Both basement slabs were inspected and found intact, with sealed penetrations and no sumps.

Opinion. Based on the sub-slab data and the attenuation and screening values adopted for this evaluation, PCE vapor migrating from the former Pellmore Cleaners source area does not present an unacceptable indoor air risk at 418 or 422 Oriel Court or at Unit 4 of the retail building. No mitigation or indoor air monitoring is warranted at these structures.

error.location_quote: Predicted indoor air concentrations at all three structures are therefore below the 47 ug/m3 screening level adopted for this evaluation.
error.explanation: The 47 ug/m3 screening level is derived for a worker exposure of 8 hours per day and 250 days per year. The memo correctly applies it to the print shop but also applies it, without adjustment, to two single-family homes, where residents are present up to 24 hours per day and about 350 days per year. Using a commercial exposure baseline for a residential scenario understates risk by a factor of about 4.2.
error.correct_reasoning: Assuming a residential exposure of 24 hours per day and 350 days per year (a common default, used here for illustration) and holding the same target risk and exposure duration, the residential equivalent is 47 x (8/24) x (250/350) = 11.2 ug/m3. Predicted indoor air of 15.6 ug/m3 at 418 Oriel Court and 18.3 ug/m3 at 422 Oriel Court exceed 11.2 ug/m3 (about 1.39 and 1.64 times). Unit 4 (42.0 ug/m3 against 47 ug/m3) remains below its commercial level. The sub-slab data, ppbv conversions, and 0.03 attenuation arithmetic are correct.
error.impact: The conclusion reverses for both residences: predicted PCE indoor air exceeds the residential-equivalent screening level, so indoor air sampling is warranted at 418 and 422 Oriel Court (with mitigation if exceedances are confirmed) rather than no action.

grading_notes: Credit requires identifying that the 47 ug/m3 value reflects an 8 hr/day, 250 day/yr worker exposure and was applied to residences without adjustment for residential exposure time and frequency, so the homes should be compared to a lower residential value. The judge need not compute the residential value (about 11 ug/m3 under common defaults) to earn credit. Near-misses that do NOT count: challenging the 0.03 attenuation factor as generic, the ppbv conversion, the canister method or leak checks, the small number of probes, or the Unit 4 commercial comparison (which is correct).

title: Boiler inhibitor cross-connection and resident illness, Thistle Row fourplex
analysis:
Consultant Memo: Boiler Inhibitor Cross-Connection and Resident Illness, Thistle Row Fourplex, 17 Tessaly Street

Purpose. Counsel for the tenants asked me to evaluate whether a cross-connection between the building's hydronic heating loop and its potable plumbing caused illness reported by residents in January.

Building and event. The fourplex is served by a single water meter and a gas-fired boiler. Make-up water to the closed heating loop is supplied from the domestic cold-water line through a reduced-pressure backflow preventer. On January 14 a heating contractor recharged the loop with a sodium nitrite and borate corrosion inhibitor. On February 3 a certified tester found the backflow preventer relief valve fouled and the device failed; the loop was isolated and the domestic lines were flushed on February 4.

Water quality. On January 23 the property manager collected first-draw kitchen tap samples. Nitrite (as N) was 1.8 mg/L in Unit 1, 2.4 mg/L in Unit 2, and 2.1 mg/L in Unit 3. The heating loop contained 610 mg/L nitrite (as N), so the highest tap value represents about 0.39 percent loop water. A January 23 sample from Unit 4, whose branch line leaves the main upstream of the boiler make-up connection, was below the 0.05 mg/L reporting limit, as was a February 6 sample from Unit 2. A notice issued January 23 told residents to stop drinking tap water.

Exposure and dose. Ingestion dose = C x IR / BW, using the January 23 concentrations. For an adult at 2.0 L/day and 70 kg, the Unit 2 concentration gives 2.4 x 2.0 / 70 = 0.069 mg/kg-day; Units 1 and 3 give 0.051 and 0.060 mg/kg-day. For the 3-year-old in Unit 2 at 1.0 L/day and 15 kg, the dose is 2.4 x 1.0 / 15 = 0.16 mg/kg-day, 1.6 times the reference dose of 0.1 mg/kg-day (as N) adopted for this evaluation.

Reported illness. Eleven people live in the building. Units 1 through 3 (8 residents) drink and cook with tap water; 6 of them reported headache, nausea, and fatigue with onset between January 16 and January 21. The 3 adults in Unit 4 use delivered bottled water for drinking and cooking; 2 of them reported the same symptoms over the same dates. All symptoms resolved by January 28, and no resident was hospitalized.

Analysis. The inhibitor was introduced on January 14, symptoms began two days later, and nitrite was confirmed in tap water from Units 1 through 3. The backflow preventer failure provides a direct pathway from the loop to the kitchen taps, and the child's dose exceeds the adopted reference dose.

Opinion. Because symptom onset in every affected resident followed the January 14 inhibitor recharge, the nitrite cross-connection caused the illnesses reported by the six residents of Units 1 through 3.

error.location_quote: Because symptom onset in every affected resident followed the January 14 inhibitor recharge, the nitrite cross-connection caused the illnesses reported by the six residents of Units 1 through 3.
error.explanation: The memo infers causation from temporal sequence alone. Its own data show that 2 of the 3 Unit 4 residents, whose tap water had no detectable nitrite and who drank and cooked with bottled water, developed the same symptoms on the same dates, so the illness rate among unexposed residents (67 percent) is close to that among exposed residents (75 percent). Adult doses (0.051 to 0.069 mg/kg-day) are also below the adopted reference dose; only the child's dose exceeds it.
error.correct_reasoning: Attack rate exposed = 6/8 = 75 percent; unexposed = 2/3 = 67 percent; relative risk = 0.75 / 0.667 = 1.13. With 11 residents this cannot distinguish an effect from no effect, and an illness rate this similar in unexposed residents points to a shared cause. Adult doses are 51 to 69 percent of the 0.1 mg/kg-day reference dose; only the Unit 2 child (0.16 mg/kg-day) exceeds it. A defensible opinion is that nitrite entered the potable supply through the failed backflow preventer and the child's exposure exceeded the adopted reference dose, but the illnesses are not attributable to the water on this record; a shared non-water cause (for example combustion gases from the same boiler work, or a circulating viral illness) must be evaluated.
error.impact: The causation opinion is unsupported and must be withdrawn; at most the contamination event and an exceedance of the adopted reference dose for one child can be stated.

grading_notes: Credit requires identifying that causation rests on timing alone and that the memo's own data undercut it: the Unit 4 residents (no detectable nitrite at their tap, bottled water for drinking and cooking) had the same symptoms over the same dates at a similar rate (2 of 3 versus 6 of 8). Noting that adult doses fall below the adopted reference dose supports this but does not earn credit on its own. Near-misses that do NOT count: questioning the dose formula, the default intake rates or body weights, the single sampling round, the reporting limit, or arguing nitrite was never present (the tap and loop data and the failed device establish the pathway).
